summary:
The Bicol Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but there is no route to legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) the Supreme Court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The Family Code confines marriage to a man and a woman, and no national statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity; the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly in Congress since 1999 without passage.

Protection in the region rests on local instruments rather than national law. Non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels, alongside sectoral statutes: the Safe Spaces Act 2019 punishes homophobic and transphobic slurs, and the Anti-Bullying Act 2013 extends SOGI coverage to basic education. Within Bicol, Albay province, which lies wholly inside the region, enacted a province-wide sexual-orientation and gender-identity anti-discrimination ordinance in 2022, one of nine provinces nationwide to do so; a trans visitor outside Albay has no sourced equivalent to rely on, and the ordinance's reach stops at the provincial boundary.

Public opinion, not statute, governs everyday exposure. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions, and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a finding that bears directly on facilities use and public presentation in Bicol even where ordinances are silent. Diversity-and-inclusion executive orders issued in 2019 and amended in 2023 exist on paper but had not been implemented as of 2025, so the formal protection machinery does not operate in practice.

No source provides a finding specific to the Bicol Region on violence, detention placement, healthcare access or police conduct. The regional assessment therefore rests on the national framework and on Albay's ordinance as the single local data point.
tangentialFactors:
Perception indices and surveys rank the Philippines among the more accepting countries in its region, and public support for an anti-discrimination law runs high. That ranking sits uneasily beside the 2018 finding that a majority of Filipinos oppose trans women's use of women's toilets, and beside the fact that national SOGI legislation has been filed repeatedly since 1999 without ever passing.

The gap between formal and effective protection recurs at every level. Executive orders on diversity and inclusion adopted in 2019 and amended in 2023 remained unimplemented as of 2025, while local non-discrimination ordinances have accumulated at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level in the absence of any national statute. Albay's 2022 ordinance belongs to that provincial tier: one of nine such ordinances nationwide, and the only one sourced for Bicol.

Local organising is visible in the region. The Gayon Albay LGBT Organization is recorded as predominantly active in the Bicol Region, indicating an established point of contact for reporting and referral, though its role in formal protection mechanisms is not sourced.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations can register with the state, and groups such as the Gayon Albay LGBT Organization operate openly in the region. Residents can invoke non-discrimination ordinances passed at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level, with Albay's 2022 province-wide ordinance the instrument in force across the territory of that province.

Schools carry obligations toward SOGI under the Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy issued in 2017 and reiterated in 2022. These provisions are resident-facing and are not framed as visitor protections.

Residents face the same documentary and marital constraints as visitors: no administrative or judicial route to a changed birth-certificate sex marker is available under RA 9048 as interpreted in the 2008 Supreme Court ruling, and marriage remains confined to a man and a woman under the Family Code.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source supplies a finding specific to the Bicol Region beyond Albay's 2022 ordinance and the presence of a regional LGBT organisation; the region's own entry in the national overview records nothing further. Violence against trans people, jail or detention placement, HIV and transition-related healthcare, restroom and establishment access, and entry or visa screening are documented nationally or for other provinces but are not sourced for Bicol, and remain unresolved for this jurisdiction.

The opinion data cited is national and dates to 2018; no regional breakdown of attitudes in Bicol is available in the inventory. Implementation of the Albay ordinance — how many complaints it has received, what penalties it carries and whether it has been enforced — is likewise not sourced.

Whether diversity-and-inclusion executive orders of 2019 and 2023 apply to agencies operating in Bicol, and what non-implementation as of 2025 means for a visitor seeking redress there, is not established by the sources.
